To connect or combine into one; to put together.

examples.text: The plumber joined the two ends of the broken pipe.
We joined our efforts to get an even better result.

glosses: To come together; to meet.

examples.text: Parallel lines never join.
These two rivers join in about 80 miles.

glosses: To enter into association or alliance, to unite in a common purpose.

examples.text:
Forſake thy king and do but ioyne with me
And we will triumph ouer al the world.

glosses: To come into the company of.

examples.text: I will join you watching the football game as soon as I have finished my work.

No matter how early I came down, I would find him on the veranda, smoking cigarettes, or otherwise his man would be there with a message to say that his master would shortly join me if I would kindly wait.

glosses: To become a member of.

examples.text: Many children join a sports club.
Most politicians have joined a party.

In the autumn there was a row at some cement works about the unskilled labour men. A union had just been started for them and all but a few joined. One of these blacklegs was laid for by a picket and knocked out of time.

glosses: To produce an intersection of data in two or more database tables.

examples.text: By joining the Customer table on the Product table, we can show each customer's name alongside the products they have ordered.

To participate or join.

examples.text: He declined to take part in the meeting because he did not feel he had anything to add.
I listened to a discussion in which she took part.
They are killed, tortured, made to take part in the fighting, banished from their homes.
Thus the revolution is that one can speak about an access to digital culture within the right to take part in cultural life.

glosses: To share or partake.

examples.text: So didst thou love man, that thou wouldest take part with him of his misery, that he might take part with thee of thy blessedness.
We have two famous tribal drums called Ntiri and Abia which are so stimulating that everybody used to take part when they sounded, but Ndiuka were educated not to dance it because it is native.

glosses: To support or ally oneself (with).

examples.text: Yet we take part, on the whole, with the author : — and heartily wish him success in the great object of vindicating his country from unmerited aspersions, and trying to make us, in England, ashamed of the vices and defects which he has taken the trouble to point out in our national character and institutions.

glosses: To be ranked at (something), based on polling.

examples.text: The Tories are on twenty-five percent in that constituency.

glosses: To be performative or funny in a wearying manner.

examples.text: You don't have to be on all the time.

glosses: To be responsible for (something).

examples.text: That task is on you.

glosses: To be up to; to be engaged in or scheduled to do imminently.

examples.text: What are you on today?

glosses: To continue in extent.

examples.text: The meeting seemed to go on forever.
This road goes on for another twenty miles.

glosses: To continue an action.

examples.text: I think I've said enough now; I'm not sure I should go on.
He went on walking even when the policeman told him to stop.
One might imagine that the directors foresaw the somewhat uninspiring appearance of the future Manchester stations, and decided to start as it was intended to go on.
She crept up the stairs [...] On she went, across the landing, from which sprang the tall window, and up the next flight until she reached the top.

glosses: To proceed (to do something).

examples.text: He started the competition badly but went on to win the gold medal.
"Do you want to hear a joke?" — "Oh, all right, go on then."
The kid who starts a business selling candy out of his locker always goes on to be a major sleazeball later in life.

glosses: To talk frequently or at great length (about a subject).

examples.text: Will you stop going on about your stupid holiday?
Sam goes on and on about Pokémon.
Don't ask Sam about Pokémon, because he'll go on and on.

"I don't believe you." I shake my head. "How on earth did you remember that? I must have told you years ago."[…]
"First of all, you go on about it far more than you think you do,[…]."

glosses: To happen (occur).

examples.text: What's going on?
I really don't want to know what goes on between you and your boyfriend behind closed doors.
At the time, with the D-Day invasion of Europe going on, their heroism was hardly noticed. Plenty of other heroes were dying elsewhere. Plenty of bigger bits of history were being made.

glosses: To move or proceed so as to become \"on\" in any of various senses.

examples.text: Bertha's about to finish her song. Who's going on next?
Smith went on for Jones at left back after Jones got injured.
It was pitch black and then suddenly all the lights went on.

glosses: Expressing that the speaker can continue speaking without interruption from the listener.

examples.text: Go on! You were saying about those other ones too?

glosses: Expressing surprise, disbelief or incredulity.

examples.text:
A: He asked Fiona to marry him.
B: Go on!
A: It's true, I swear.

glosses: Expressing encouragement, see come on.

examples.text: Go on! You can do it!

glosses: Yes; okay; it's a deal.

examples.text:
—So three hundred on the chair then, and can we do two-fifty on the clock?
—Go on, then.

glosses: To use and adopt (information) in order to understand an issue, make a decision, etc.; to go by.

examples.text: We can't go on what this map says; it's twenty years out of date.
I didn't make a decision because I didn't have anything to go on.
